passage: In the architecture studio, Professor Menon stopped at Gautam's model and actually smiled. "Look at this light well, everyone. This is how you think about a courtyard." Twenty students crowded round. Jaya stood at the back. It was good; she could see that. The folded roof, the way the light fell. Something tightened under her ribs. "The glue's showing at the corners," she said, a little too loud. "And the scale figures are wrong. Those people would be three metres tall." A few people laughed. Gautam's ears went red. Later, back at her own desk, Jaya stared at her plain box of a model. She had spent the same three weeks. Why did his look like that? She peeled a strip of tape off her roof, then pressed it back.

qa.q: What did Jaya say about the scale figures?
qa.a: That they were wrong and those people would be three metres tall.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when something tightened under her ribs?
qa.a: Jaya admired the model but felt a sting of envy and fear of falling behind, which came out as criticism.

qa.q: What could Jaya do the next time that tight feeling comes, instead of pointing out faults?
qa.a: Jaya could notice the feeling, admit the work is good, and perhaps ask Gautam how the light well was designed.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt when the others laughed?
qa.a: Gautam's red ears suggest embarrassment; a moment of praise was spoiled by a classmate's public nitpicking.

grounding: A student feels envy when a classmate's model is praised and publicly picks small faults in it.

passage:
Hi Rehana,
Big news from college: Harleen got the Tokyo exchange scholarship. Everyone's congratulating her like she cured something.
Honestly? Her essay wasn't that great. I read it; she used 'passionate' four times. And she only got the interview because Professor Bhalla likes her. Also, she can't even use chopsticks properly, which is funny for someone going to Japan.
I applied too, you know. I didn't tell anyone. The rejection mail came the same morning the list went up.
I know I sound petty. I used to think Harleen was the most interesting person in our batch. I still sort of do. That's what's annoying.
Anyway, how's Pune?
Jyoti

qa.q: How many times did Harleen's essay use 'passionate', according to Jyoti?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What feelings show when Jyoti writes "That's what's annoying"?
qa.a: Jyoti still admires Harleen, and that stings; the rejection on the same morning turned admiration into envy and fault-finding.

qa.q: Jyoti admits sounding petty. What could Jyoti choose to do with that honesty?
qa.a: Jyoti could admit the rejection hurt, perhaps to Rehana, and congratulate Harleen sincerely instead of collecting small faults.

qa.q: How might Rehana read this email?
qa.a: Rehana may see past the jokes to how much the quiet rejection hurt Jyoti, and might gently ask about it.

grounding: A young adult picks small faults in a classmate who won a scholarship, while admitting envy after a quiet rejection of their own.

passage: You know what I did last week, Salma? I'm not proud of it. At the call centre, the team lead put Deepa's name on the board, 'Agent of the Month,' with a gold star. Deepa joined after me. Everyone clapped, and I clapped too, but my face felt hot. Then at tea break I said, 'Well, she takes the easy calls, no? Billing questions.' And, 'She reads straight off the script.' Small things. Nothing that was even untrue, exactly. But I watched people nod and look at her differently. The thing is, I used to go to Deepa when I got stuck. She's good. I think I was scared that I, Kiran, would be stuck in the same seat forever while she moved up.

qa.q: What did the team lead put on the board?
qa.a: Deepa's name, 'Agent of the Month,' with a gold star.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's face feel hot during the clapping?
qa.a: Kiran felt envy and fear of being left behind, since Deepa joined later and was praised first.

qa.q: Looking back, what choice could Kiran have made at the tea break?
qa.a: Kiran could have admitted the sting privately and said something true and kind, like how Deepa helps when people get stuck.

qa.q: How might Deepa be affected if people start looking at her differently?
qa.a: Deepa might feel colleagues cooling without knowing why, right after a moment that should have felt good.

grounding: A young adult feels a sting when a colleague is praised and quietly mentions small faults to others.

passage: I'm Zeenat, and I've shared a hostel room with Tanuja since first year of nursing college. On Monday the principal read out Pooja's village health camp report at assembly and called it "the standard for the batch." Everyone clapped. Tanuja clapped, but I saw her jaw go tight. Back in the room she said, "Nice handwriting, that's all it is." Later, over rice in the mess, she mentioned twice that Pooja had spelled "haemoglobin" wrong on page three. I hadn't even noticed. On Wednesday, when a junior asked Pooja for help with her own report, Tanuja said, "Ask me, I'll tell you what not to copy." She laughed after, but it didn't sound like a laugh. I can't say what was going on inside her. Tanuja and Pooja used to study together every night.

qa.q: How long has Zeenat shared a hostel room with Tanuja?
qa.a: Since first year of nursing college.

qa.q: What might Tanuja's tight jaw and forced laugh suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: They suggest the praise for Pooja stung her, perhaps with envy or fear of being left behind, which comes out as criticism.

qa.q: How could Tanuja respond differently the next time a batchmate is praised?
qa.a: She could admit to herself that it stings, congratulate Pooja, and ask how the report came together, instead of hunting for errors.

qa.q: How might Pooja be affected if she hears Tanuja's remarks?
qa.a: Pooja might feel hurt and confused, since they used to study together every night, and may pull away from Tanuja.

grounding: A roommate observes a young adult feel stung by a peer's praise and point out small faults.

passage:
Day one. Sabina's team won the college hackathon, and the dean shook her hand on stage. Karthik, who had spent months on his own app and never finished it, clapped hard and texted her: "Deserved!" He meant it. Mostly.
Day three. In the canteen, Professor Rao said Sabina's code was "the cleanest I've seen from a second-year." Karthik heard himself say, "Her slides had a typo, though. And she only did the front end." The table went quiet. He looked at his tea.
Day seven. Karthik opened his laptop at midnight. His own app folder hadn't been touched since August. Sabina had already been offered an internship. He scrolled through the folder, then closed it again, jaw tight, and typed into his notes: Why did I say that about the slides?

qa.q: When did Karthik's app folder last get touched?
qa.a: It hadn't been touched since August.

qa.q: Why might Karthik have mentioned the typo and the front end?
qa.a: Seeing Sabina praised again, while his own app sat unfinished, seems to have stirred envy and a fear of falling behind that came out as criticism.

qa.q: What small step could Karthik take after writing that question in his notes?
qa.a: He could admit the envy to himself, apologise lightly to the table, and spend the energy on finishing his own app.

qa.q: How might the others at the table see Karthik after his remarks?
qa.a: They might be surprised, since he had congratulated her before, and they may start to think of him as petty.

grounding: A young adult's admiration for a praised peer turns into fault-finding driven by envy and fear of being left behind.
